name: PT Mahkota Group Tbk

frontmatter.title: MGRO — a leveraged palm refiner priced as an option
frontmatter.summary: MGRO buys CPO, PK and FFB and refines them on a thin, cyclical spread. The equity is a levered claim on that spread: net debt of IDR1,790.0bn less IDR46.2bn of cash at the last balance sheet against FY2026E EBITDA of 350.9, a DCF equity of Rp113 per share, and a price 2.5 times the discounted fundamental of Rp279. We rate the shares REDUCE with a target of Rp609.
thesis: The business is a pass-through refiner, not an estate. FY2025 gross margin was 6.2% and EBITDA margin 1.9%; margins swing with the CPO cycle, not with volume, and volume has grown while profit has not [S5].

Leverage dominates the equity. Net debt of IDR1,790.0bn less IDR46.2bn of cash at the 30 September 2026 balance sheet against FY2026E EBITDA of 350.9 and parent equity of Rp404.9bn leaves the DCF equity worth Rp113 a share, so a small enterprise-value move swings the per-share value in both directions [S0, S11].

The cash-flow value is positive but thin, not zero. Our DCF enterprise value of Rp2,189.2bn clears borrowing of IDR1,790.0bn less IDR46.2bn of cash by a margin the equity multiplies into Rp113 a share; the peer EV/EBITDA cross-check still floors, at 6.0x trailing EBITDA, and the book method gives Rp136 [S0].

The market pays 14.2x forward EV/EBITDA and 6.0x book for a refiner with no plantation base, no dividend and a free float of 10.2%; today's price implies a CPO benchmark of US$1,285/t, above the FY2027E deck [S0, S12].

We rate the shares REDUCE with a target of Rp609, a return of -13.0%. The fundamental probability-weighted value is Rp319 and the target keeps only part of the premium, because a concentrated register slows convergence [S12].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: confirmation that the second-half margin recovery is a spread, not a one-off
Biodiesel mandate step-up and the monthly CPO export-levy schedule, both of which reset domestic demand and the levy line
GAPKI export and output statistics: FFB supply into the mills and the export share of sales
Annual free-float and high-concentration review; any change in the register is the main non-fundamental driver

blocks.text: We initiate on MGRO with a REDUCE rating and a twelve-month target of Rp609, against a price of 700.0: a return of -13.0%. The fundamental probability-weighted value is Rp319, and the gap between that and the target is deliberate — the target assumes only part of the current premium closes within a year, while the fundamental value assumes it closes in full [S0, S12]. The valuation rests on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet as the filing states it: total borrowing of IDR1,790.0bn, cash of IDR46.2bn and the group's own net debt of IDR1,514.7bn after restricted funds — the cash-only figure this model bridges is that total borrowing less the cash — not the larger figure the data pack carried [S11]. Our base scenario is worth Rp101 per share, the bear case Rp23 and the bull case Rp1,050, with the base carrying half the probability.

The variant view is about what the equity is. MGRO is not a plantation: it buys crude palm oil, palm kernel and fresh fruit bunches and sells refined products on a spread. FY2025 revenue was Rp6,332.1bn on 411.8 kt sold, cost of revenue Rp5,941.0bn, gross profit Rp391.1bn and EBITDA Rp118.8bn; the net result was a loss of Rp-56.8bn [S5]. The spread is procyclical — gross margin was 9.7% at the FY2022 price peak and 4.7% in the FY2023 trough — and the market is capitalising the peak of that spread, not the through-cycle level [S0, S5].

Leverage is the second half of the argument. Net debt was Rp1,918.8bn at the last audited date and is IDR1,790.0bn less IDR46.2bn of cash at the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, against FY2026E EBITDA of 350.9 and parent equity of Rp404.9bn [S0, S11]. At that gearing the enterprise value, not the profit, sets the share price: our DCF enterprise value of Rp2,189.2bn clears net debt, but only by a margin the equity multiplies into Rp113 a share, while the peer EV/EBITDA method still floors at 6.0x trailing EBITDA and the book method gives Rp136 [S0].

Three things move the value from here. First, the CPO spread: a wider spread lifts enterprise value and the equity is a levered claim on it. Second, the export channel, which collapsed in 2026 and took the levy line with it; a rebound would add cost as well as revenue [S11]. Third, the register: with 80.1% held by insiders and a free float of 10.2%, price discovery is thin and the premium can persist longer than fundamentals justify [S12].

MGRO is an Indonesian palm-oil processor. It purchases crude palm oil, palm kernel and fresh fruit bunches from third parties and smallholders, and sells refined, bleached and deodorised palm oil, palm fatty acid distillate, crude palm kernel oil, palm kernel expeller, olein, stearin and palm kernel meal. FY2025 sales were 411.8 kt of products against 584.4 kt of production; the difference is tolling and third-party processing, where the group runs material through its mills and refinery for other owners rather than selling it on its own account [S5].

The asset base is processing, not land. The group operates three mills, a refinery with two lines after the second line at its refinery subsidiary started up, storage tanks, and only a small own estate of under a thousand hectares, which supplies a fraction of the fruit it processes [S5]. Capacity is not the constraint: production has run well above the tonnage the group sells on its own account, so incremental volume comes from winning third-party supply and from utilisation, not from planting [S5, F10].

The sales mix is domestic-first. In FY2025 domestic sales were 75.0% of revenue and exports 25.0% [S5], and through the first nine months of 2026 the export share collapsed to a low single-digit percentage of revenue as domestic oleochemical and food buyers absorbed output [S5, S11]. That shift matters for costs: the export levy is booked in selling expenses, so the smaller export channel took the levy line down with it even as revenue grew [S11].

Ownership is concentrated. Insiders hold 80.1% and the free float is 10.2%, and the register has been described publicly as controlled by a small number of parties [S0, S12]. The group employed 1,233.0 people at the last count [S0]. Strategy is downstream integration — refinery capacity, an integrated agro-industry project and tank logistics — rather than estate expansion, which is the right reading of a processor that owns almost no planted area [S5]. The customer base is domestic refiners, oleochemical producers and food manufacturers, and the group's own brand presence is negligible, so the sales book is won on price, specification and delivery reliability rather than on a consumer franchise [S5]. That position is consistent with a business that processes other parties' material as well as its own and earns a fee-like spread on throughput [S5].

The product is priced off the CPO deck. Our agri deck has CPO at US$1,135/t in FY2026E, US$1,240/t in FY2027E, easing to US$1,180/t by FY2029E and a long-run anchor of US$1,150/t; the spot print is US$1,180/t [S0]. Indonesia is the largest palm producer and the marginal supplier to the world market, so the rupiah price of palm products is set by a dollar price, an export levy and the exchange rate, none of which a refiner of MGRO's size can influence [S5, S13].

Regulation runs through the levy and the biodiesel mandate. The export levy is charged per tonne at shipment and was cut for November, which changes the cost of the export channel and the incentive to sell domestically [S13]. The biodiesel mandate sets a growing share of domestic palm oil into fuel, which supports domestic demand for refined product but also competes with MGRO for the crude oil it buys [S13]. MGRO's scale makes it a price-taker on both sides: it buys at the same reference price as every other refiner and sells at a discount to the benchmark that reflects its product mix [S5].

Competitive position is weak. The group has no plantation base to capture the upstream margin, no brand in consumer products, and no logistics network beyond its own tanks; its advantage is permits, refining capacity and the relationships that bring third-party fruit and crude oil to its mills [S5]. Barriers to entry in refining are capital and permits, not technology, and Indonesian refining capacity has been built out faster than domestic demand, which keeps the processing spread competitive [S5]. The practical consequence is that the group cannot earn a cost-plus price: it takes the reference price on both sides and competes for third-party supply on service and turnaround, which is why its margin is a throughput spread rather than a rental on assets.

On any measure of national output MGRO's tonnage is a rounding error, so its market share says something about its cost position and nothing about pricing power [S5]. Five forces, briefly: supplier power is low because smallholders and traders are fragmented, but it rises in a short crop; buyer power is high because domestic oleochemical and food buyers are large and can import; the threat of substitutes sits in competing vegetable oils, which cap palm's premium; new entry is possible but uneconomic at current spreads; and rivalry is high, with refiners competing for third-party crude and fruit. The moat is essentially nil, and the correct valuation frame is a spread on throughput rather than a franchise [S5].

El Nino conditions are the classic supply shock for palm: a sustained dry spell delays fruit development and lowers yields a year or more later, and industry bodies have warned that Indonesian output could fall meaningfully in the next crop year. For a processor that buys its raw material, a short crop is a volume and cost risk rather than a revenue benefit, because the group has almost no own estate to sell the higher price from.

The FY2025 accounts are the anchor. Revenue of Rp6,332.1bn produced cost of revenue of Rp5,941.0bn, gross profit of Rp391.1bn (6.2%), operating expenses of Rp374.1bn, EBIT of Rp17.0bn and a net loss of Rp-56.8bn, of which Rp-48.3bn was attributable to the parent [S5]. The gross margin was 6.2% against 9.7% at the FY2022 price peak and 7.5% the year before, so the last audited year was mid-cycle rather than a peak, and the operating expense line consumed most of what was left, which is the structural problem with this business [S5].

Depreciation is the main restatement. The data pack carries a depreciation figure taken from the direct-method cash-flow statement that is a fraction of the actual charge; we restate it from the fixed-asset note at IDR101.8bn for FY2025 and IDR91.1bn for FY2024, which rebuilds EBITDA at Rp118.8bn rather than the pack's misleadingly small number [S0, S5, F7, F8]. We checked for a PSAK 16 revaluation uplift and found none, so book value is not inflated by a revaluation reserve [S5].

The 2026 trend is better but not different in kind. Nine-month revenue of IDR6,555.3bn exceeded the whole of FY2025, gross profit of IDR365.0bn on that revenue was a lower margin than the FY2025 6.2% rather than a higher one, and the group returned to a net profit after the prior year's loss; selling and general expenses together ran at a lower share of revenue than in FY2025 because the export channel, and the levy inside it, shrank [S11]. That nine-month margin is the measure the calibration note answers to: it is total COGS against total revenue, not the CPO segment's own cost base, which is about half a percentage point too generous [S11 p.129].

Working capital is why cash did not follow profit. Cash fell to IDR46.2bn at the end of September, but borrowing fell too, to IDR1,790.0bn at the end of September from Rp2,096.1bn at the December 2025 year-end, so net debt fell over the nine months rather than rising; the improvement in profit was funded by a working-capital release and by the lower levy bill, not by new debt [S11, S0].

The forecast is above the nine-month run rate only in the fourth quarter, and the step is visible. FY2026E revenue of Rp8,886.8bn against IDR6,555.3bn for the nine months implies a fourth quarter close to the nine-month quarterly average rather than far above it; the EBITDA step is in the margin, with FY2026E EBITDA of Rp350.9bn at a margin of 3.9% against a nine-month margin a fraction lower, carried at the FY2025 full-year gross margin of 6.2% because the last audited year closed there after a weaker nine months — its fourth quarter was the weakest of that year, at a fifth of annual revenue — and because the November export-levy cut lowers the selling charge in this one [S11, S13].

Our forecast reproduces the last actual's economics at the deck's prices. FY2026E revenue is Rp8,886.8bn on 480.0 kt at a realisation of 92.8% of the CPO benchmark, cash cost of IDR17.1m per tonne, EBITDA of Rp350.9bn, EBIT of Rp229.3bn and net profit of Rp103.5bn, of which Rp58.1bn is attributable to the parent — parent earnings per share of Rp16.6, on the post-buyback share count of 3,488.4m [S0, S11]. Volume grows to 520.0 kt on refinery utilisation and then flattens; the cap is sourced, not assumed. FY2025 production was 584.4 kt against 411.8 kt of own-account sales, and the distance between the two is not captive volume waiting to be converted: production counts refined output from purchased FFB as well as purchased CPO, while sales count products sold, so part of the gap is the FFB-to-product conversion itself and part is tolling for other owners, which earns a fee rather than a product margin [S5, F10]. Converting a tolling tonne to an own-account tonne adds revenue and an almost identical cost, so it would not add EBITDA, and the plan already assumes sales grow faster than the group's own estate could support — the growth comes from winning third-party crude and fruit, not from planting [S5].

Tax and realisation are the two assumptions where the filings point the other way from caution. Tax is carried at 15.0%: the group booked a tax benefit on the FY2025 loss and a benefit again in the nine-month period, so the carried-forward losses shield near-term profit, and a normalised rate above the effective rate the accounts show and below the statutory rate is the through-cycle charge rather than a haircut — the shield is upside to the model, not a base assumption [S0, S5, S11]. Realisation is held at the FY2025 ratio because the downstream strategy the group describes has not yet moved the blended price: 9M2026 revenue on the modelled volume implies the same blended price per tonne as FY2025, so an integration uplift is a thesis to be sourced from a future period, not a number to put in this one [S5, S11].

Cash flow is the weak link. FY2026E free cash flow to the firm is negative at Rp-442.1bn because working capital absorbs the revenue growth, and capex of Rp250.0bn — of which the expansion line at the refinery subsidiary is carried separately, on the 9M2026 fixed-asset-addition run rate — runs ahead of depreciation of Rp121.6bn, even though capex is only a small share of revenue [S0, S5, S11]. Interest of Rp113.2bn absorbs most of EBIT, which is why a business with positive EBITDA can report a small net profit and negative equity free cash flow at the same time [S0].

The balance sheet is the binding constraint, but less tightly than the pack implied. Net debt at the 30 September 2026 balance sheet is IDR1,514.7bn on the group's own definition after restricted funds, and on our cash-only convention the borrowing of IDR1,790.0bn less IDR46.2bn of cash, against FY2026E EBITDA of 350.9; parent equity is Rp404.9bn and the group has no committed refinancing disclosed in the interim filing [S0, S11]. The engine's own FY2026E net-debt line of Rp2,452.3bn is higher because it still carries the December 2025 debt balance and the full-year cash build; we use the balance-sheet figure for leverage and in the bridge. Interest cover is thin, the debt is bank and medium-term-note finance rather than bonds, and the maturity profile is not disclosed in the nine-month report — a disclosure gap we flag rather than model around [S11].

Earnings quality. The reported loss is not an accrual artefact: operating cash flow was positive in FY2025 while the P&L showed a loss, and the three-year pattern of losses has been accompanied by working-capital build rather than by receivables or inventory outgrowing revenue abnormally [S0, S11]. Related-party purchases were 0.7% of cost of revenue in the first nine months of 2026, down sharply from the prior year, so related-party gravity is small at the purchases line though it remains a governance item to monitor [S11]. There is no dividend — the last was paid in 2022 — and parent equity carries negative retained earnings, so the dividend-capacity anchor gives nothing [S0].

This is a commodity processor, so the method set is a through-cycle DCF as primary with an EV/EBITDA and a P/B cross-check. The DCF is the right primary because the value is a spread on throughput that must be discounted over the asset life; the multiple cross-checks are there because a cyclical's cash flow is a poor single-year signal and because the equity's value depends on where enterprise value sits relative to debt [S0].

The cost of capital is built from the macro deck, not from a company regression. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2%, the country risk premium 2.5%, the unlevered beta 0.80 (the industry default, since no plantation regression exists in the house universe), giving a levered beta of 1.26 at a debt-to-equity of 0.73, a cost of equity of 14.2% and a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% [S0]. The weights are 57.7% equity and 42.3% debt, which produces a WACC of 11.3%.

The cost of debt needs one reconciliation, because the model uses two rates for two different jobs. The WACC uses the marginal rate the macro deck implies — the risk-free rate plus the Indonesian corporate debt spread — which is what a refinancing of the whole debt stack would cost today. The interest line uses 5.4%, the embedded rate the FY2025 accounts show (finance cost over opening debt) on bank loans and medium-term notes [S0, S5]. The two are not interchangeable: the embedded rate is a historical average on facilities already drawn, and the section on refinancing risk says the group rolls unsecured lines against cash of IDR46.2bn. Discounting FCFF at the embedded rate would assume the entire stack refinances at its own history, which is the one assumption the liquidity risk section rejects; discounting at the marginal rate while charging interest at the embedded rate is the conservative-but-coherent pairing, and the DCF at the embedded rate would be materially higher again.

The DCF runs six explicit years. The CPO deck is year-by-year only to FY2029E and then offers a single long-run anchor, so we start the terminal value where the sourced price path stops rather than discounting a decade of one long-run price; volume is flat after FY2030E and the terminal growth is the deck's long-run rupiah inflation [S0]. On that basis the discounted cash flows are worth Rp2,189.2bn of enterprise value, of which 76.7% is terminal value. The bridge to the equity is stated in full: enterprise value, less net debt at the 30 September 2026 balance sheet of IDR1,790.0bn less IDR46.2bn of cash, less minority interests and plus the group's associates stake. The net-debt line in the bridge is the valuation-date balance, not the FY2026E forecast line of Rp2,452.3bn, which still carries the December 2025 debt balance and a full-year cash build; the engine bridges the filing's balance sheet instead, and that restatement is what turns a floored method into a positive one. The result is a DCF equity value of Rp113 per share: the enterprise value clears the debt stack by a margin the equity multiplies, and the margin is thin enough that the leverage still drives the per-share answer [S0, S11].

The truncation date is a choice, and it is the weakest part of the method. A terminal value that starts where a six-year price path stops is a function of the date, not of the asset: the refinery, mills and tanks have book lives well beyond the explicit window and no depleting reserve, so the 76.7% terminal share is the price we pay for using sourced prices rather than a decade of one anchor. We disclose it rather than extend it: the terminal value capitalises the last explicit-year cash flow at the spread between a WACC of 11.3% and terminal growth of 2.5%, so a hundred basis points on the discount rate moves the enterprise value by about a tenth, and the DCF clears net debt with or without the truncation. The asset-life statement is that this is a processing asset with no reserve life; a net-asset-value approach is not the natural frame, so the cost-curve question is answered by the spread: MGRO is a price-taker at both ends and its position on the industry cost curve is set by throughput utilisation, not by a resource position [S0, S5].

The cross-checks disagree with the primary and with each other. The EV/EBITDA method applies a peer multiple of 6.0 to trailing EBITDA — the last reported fiscal year, which is the number the method is configured to use, not the FY2026E forecast balance — and produces an enterprise value that does not clear net debt, so it values the equity at Rp0 and is floored [S0]. The P/B method applies 1.3 to parent book value and gives Rp136 per share: the balance-sheet floor, which survives because it does not depend on the spread at all [S0]. That multiple is the peer median, and it is deliberately not the company's own four-year average: a mean of the 2021-22 palm-boom and konglo-premium multiples is a statement about the regime, and putting it into the fundamental value would count the premium twice — once here and once in the regime lens below. The arithmetic matters: at the peer median the whole equity is worth about a fifth of the market's book multiple, and at the blended multiple the book alone would have supplied the entire fundamental value. The book method earns a 15% weight because it is a floor, not a fair value; it says what the balance sheet is worth, not what the spread is worth.

We weight the methods 60% DCF, 25% EV/EBITDA and 15% P/B, which lands at a fundamental value of Rp319 per share. The twelve-month target of Rp609 then applies the konglo lens, because the shares meet the regime test: they are on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, the free float is 10.2% against a 15.0% minimum, and the stock is outside the headline indices [S0, S12]. The two ratios the lens runs on are different numbers and the difference matters: the price of Rp700 is 2.5 times the discounted today-value of our fundamental (Rp279 a share, which is Rp319 twelve months out discounted back at the cost of equity), and it stands above the undiscounted twelve-month fundamental of Rp319 by a smaller margin. The premium-kept factor multiplies the twelve-month fundamental, not the discounted value: the base case closes 35.0% of the log gap over twelve months, so the target sits between the fundamental value and today's price rather than at either [S0, S12]. The regime scenarios run from Rp401 to Rp877, and the lens is a statement about how fast a concentrated register lets the price converge, not a second fundamental view [S12].

Sensitivity is dominated by the spread and by leverage, not by the discount rate. A change in the CPO benchmark moves revenue and, with a lag, the input cost, so the effect on the equity is a second-order function of the margin; a change in the multiple moves enterprise value against a fixed debt stack, which is where the convexity comes from — and with the equity worth less than a fifth of enterprise value, a small percentage move in enterprise value is a large percentage move in the target [S0].

What today's price implies is a spread, not a share value. Running the DCF backwards on the FY2027E deck, the current price is consistent with a CPO benchmark of US$1,285/t against the deck's US$1,240/t for that year — the market is paying 42.1x forward earnings and 14.2x forward EV/EBITDA, and requires either the benchmark to clear the deck or the cost of capital to fall, at the same time, for a business whose through-cycle cash flow barely covers its debt [S0]. The reverse DCF therefore describes a price that needs a spread recovery and a lower cost of capital together, or a strategic buyer; neither is in our base case [S0].

The largest risk is liquidity and refinancing, and it is structural rather than cyclical. Borrowing of IDR1,790.0bn at the last balance sheet against cash of IDR46.2bn, no disclosed maturity profile in the interim filing and negative free cash flow in the growth year mean the group depends on rolling bank lines; a refinancing at a wider spread would hit the equity before it hit EBITDA [S0, S11]. Likelihood is medium and impact is high.

The commodity and FX risks are the same risk seen twice. MGRO's margin is the difference between a dollar-denominated selling price and a rupiah cost base that moves with the CPO price and the exchange rate, so a rupiah depreciation helps revenue and hurts the purchased input at the same time; the net effect is a spread effect, not a translation effect [S5, S13]. A short crop from El Nino conditions is a volume risk for a processor with almost no estate of its own.

Regulatory risk is real but second-order. The export levy is reset monthly and the biodiesel mandate is stepping up, both of which change the domestic-export mix and the levy line inside selling expenses; a reversal of the export-levy cut would raise the cost of the export channel that has already shrunk [S13, S11].

Governance and structure risks are the register, the free float and the related-party line. The register is concentrated, the free float is 10.2%, and related-party purchases, while small at 0.7% of cost of revenue now, have been larger; a change in control or a related-party transaction is the main non-fundamental way value can move [S12, S11].

The scenarios are mirrored on the same drivers, and the honest limitation is stated first: the peer EV/EBITDA method still floors at zero, and the third method values a book that a one-year earnings shock barely moves, so the bear sits close to the book floor while the base no longer does. That is a property of a levered equity whose enterprise value sits just above its debt, not a claim that a bad year leaves the shares untouched. The bear values the shares at Rp23, the base at Rp101 and the bull, where the enterprise value moves well clear of the debt stack, at Rp1,050. The probability-weighted value still leans on the bull: 25.0% of the weight carries most of the distance from the floor, and a reader who thinks the bull is less likely than a quarter should treat the fundamental value as closer to the base case than to the weighted figure [S0].

The bear case itself takes CPO to four-fifths of the deck and lets the purchased input fall by less than the selling price, so the spread compresses rather than the margin holding; volumes five per cent below plan as the El Nino shortfall tightens FFB supply; and the opex ratio a quarter higher, carried at 3.6% times the bear multiplier, because an export revival on the levy cut carries the levy line back into selling expenses against a smaller revenue base [S13]. The bull takes CPO a fifth higher, lets the input cost lag, adds five per cent volume and lets the domestic-first mix hold the opex ratio down by the mirrored amount. The four shocks are mirrored in both directions, and the weights are re-tested after the balance-sheet correction rather than carried over: a quarter bear, a half base and a quarter bull remains the honest statement, because the shocks are symmetric, the base is the single most likely path at half the weight, and the quarter on the bull is the probability that the deck's own price path — already above spot — is exceeded for a sustained period [S0, S13].

The two risks the scenarios cannot carry are carried here instead, and named. The first is refinancing. The bear shocks prices, volume and cost but not the debt, because the engine rolls the whole stack at the embedded rate in every scenario; a two-hundred-basis-point widening on the IDR1,790.0bn stack is real cash cost that no scenario in the table contains, and it would land on the equity before it landed on EBITDA. We do not model it as a separate scenario because that would break the mirror rule — the bull would need a mirror tightening the group cannot engineer — so it sits as the largest single downside alongside the book floor, and the signpost is a disclosed maturity schedule [S0, S11].

The second is the El Nino supply shock, and it cuts the other way from the price-fall bear. A short crop raises the price of the fruit and crude oil MGRO buys while lowering the volume it can process, so the loss is in the spread and in utilisation, not in the selling price; a scenario that runs volume down, cost up and the benchmark up is a different state from a price-fall recession, and the engine's three-scenario structure can hold only one of them. We keep the price-fall case in the table, where it mirrors the bull, and record the supply case as the competing downside: GAPKI's warning is quantified at up to three million tonnes of national output, and for a processor with almost no estate the whole of that risk arrives through purchased FFB and crude oil rather than through lost own-crop revenue [S5, S11].

The konglo lens is the second non-fundamental driver and it cuts both ways. The shares are on the high-shareholding-concentration list, sit outside the headline indices, and carry a free-float gap of 4.8% that must close by the regulatory deadline; if the register widens or the index exclusion reverses, the premium can compress faster than the base case assumes, which is why the regime bear value is Rp401 [S12, S0]. The opposite is also possible: a squeeze in a thin float can hold the price above value for longer than a fundamental investor expects, which is the regime bull value of Rp877 [S12].

Signposts that would change our view: a sustained gross margin above the FY2022 peak on the audited accounts; a reduction in net debt through asset sales or a rights issue with a credible use of proceeds; a disclosed refinancing that extends maturities at the current cost of debt; or a change in the register that raises the free float [S5, S11, S12]. Each would move us toward the bull case; the absence of any of them keeps us at REDUCE [S0].

Ownership and control are concentrated. Insiders hold 80.1% of the shares and the free float is 10.2%, and the company has been cited in the press as one of the names whose register is controlled by a small number of parties [S0, S12]. The controller is nameable: the ultimate parent is PT Mahkota Global Investama [S11], and the main shareholders are the Sarsi family [S5]; our konglo registry carries the name on the high-concentration list but its group field is empty, because the registry maps a group's listed members and MGRO is the family's only listed vehicle we hold — the group role is that of a family holding company over a single listed processor, not a member of a multi-listed conglomerate. That structure is the main reason the target sits above the fundamental value: convergence is slow when so little stock trades [S12].

Related-party exposure is modest at the operating line but persistent. Purchases of raw materials from related parties were 0.7% of cost of revenue in the first nine months of 2026, down from a materially higher share a year earlier, and related-party revenue was a fraction of one per cent of the total [S11]. We treat the related-party line as an item to monitor rather than a manipulation-class flag, and we found no evidence of fabricated cash or fictitious revenue in the sources we reviewed [S0, S5, S11].

The dividend record is bare. The last dividend was paid in 2022, the parent has accumulated losses, and our forecast assumes no payout, so there is no dividend-capacity anchor for the valuation [S0, S5]. The buyback that reduced the share count to 3,488.4m shares is complete, and we model no further reduction [S0].

The regime flags are the governance facts that matter most for the share price. The company is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, which keeps it out of the IHSG calculation and out of the main index families, and its free float of 10.2% is below the 15.0% minimum, with a gap of 4.8% and a deadline roughly two and a half years out [S0, S12]. There is no enforcement action or index deletion recorded against the company in our registry, and HSC status is a disclosure status rather than a finding of wrongdoing; the risk is flow, not fraud [S12].

Two governance items are open rather than resolved. We have not yet verified the identity of the audit firm and the audit opinion from the annual report, and we could not confirm the exchange's board and notation status for the shares from a registered source, because exchange pages are outside the fetch registry; both are gaps for the next review, not findings [S5]. The pledge disclosure is printed, not missing: the interim accounts record that the shares in the refinery subsidiary PT Intan Sejati Andalan are pledged, together with a fiduciary transfer of inventory securing the group's bank facilities [S11]. A pledge over the refinery subsidiary's equity is the structure flag that matters here — it sits ahead of the listed parent in a default, and it means the book value the P/B method capitalises is not freely available to the listed shareholder.

ESG exposure is concentrated in the supply chain. The group's own planted area is small, so the deforestation question sits with the third-party fruit and crude oil it buys; its mills and refinery carry the usual effluent, methane and energy exposures, and certification of third-party supply is the practical constraint on selling to European buyers [S5]. The domestic-first sales mix reduces near-term certification pressure but also reduces the upside from premium export markets [S11].

Indonesian palm processors sit between smallholders and a concentrated downstream buyer base, and the sector's ESG scrutiny has shifted from own-estate deforestation to the traceability of third-party fruit. For a processor with negligible planted area, the practical ESG risk is a customer or financier demanding traceability it cannot document, rather than a land-title dispute of its own.

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 audited results in March, the January step-up in the biodiesel mandate and the monthly export-levy schedule, and the annual free-float and concentration review in the middle of the year [S5, S13, S12]. The FY2026 accounts matter most because they will show whether the second-half margin recovery is a spread phenomenon or a one-off, and whether the working-capital build reverses [S11].

Between updates we watch four KPIs: the realised spread, measured as revenue per tonne against cash cost per tonne; the export share of revenue and the levy line inside selling expenses; net debt against EBITDA; and the free float and register [S11, S12]. A widening spread with falling net debt would move us toward the bull case; a widening spread funded by more debt would not [S11].

The final monitoring item is disclosure. A maturity schedule for the debt, a statement on the audit opinion and any related-party transaction above a materiality threshold would close the gaps we have flagged, and any of them could change the risk assessment without changing the earnings forecast [S11, S5].

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for MGRO.JK

S12.title: Saham TCPI dan MGRO dikuasai segelintir pihak

S13.title: Beban ekspor CPO turun 20 persen di November

bear.narrative: A spread squeeze rather than a price collapse: palm prices give back a fifth, the purchased-CPO cost falls only fifteen per cent because raw-material costs are sticky on the way down, and the gross margin lands near the FY2023 trough. The export channel revives on the November-2026 levy cut [S13] and the levy line, which sits in selling expenses, rises against a revenue base a fifth smaller, so the opex ratio takes a quarter step up (a.opex_pct x1.25, the mirror of the bull x0.8); volumes run five per cent below plan as the GAPKI El Nino shortfall tightens FFB supply, which is the same channel that raises the input cost. Debt is rolled at a wider spread. The bear is now valued on its own enterprise value: the corrected bridge leaves room for a positive DCF equity in the bear case, so the book multiple is no longer the only live method.

bull.narrative: An El Nino supply squeeze lifts CPO a fifth, as 2021-22 did, and purchased-CPO costs lag the selling price so the gross margin widens toward the FY2022 peak against the FY2025 level [S0]. Refinery line-2 and a second shift let volume run 5% above plan. The export mix stays domestic-first, so the levy line does not grow with a revenue base twenty per cent larger and the opex ratio eases (a.opex_pct x0.8) [S11].

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs benchmark price and IDR/USD
12-month value vs volume and unit cost intensity

adjustments.why: on the exchange's HSC list (as of 2026-10-22): out of the IHSG, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and the MSCI indexes [konglo deck S3]

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

OPS.label: Cash cost + royalty per unit (price currency)

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan (kt of products)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 actual 411.787 kt [F1] and FY2024 342.705 kt [F2] are the base. FY2026E of 480 kt is the 9M-2026 revenue path converted at the modelled blended ASP: 9M revenue was Rp6,555.3bn [S11] and Q4 is set at roughly the Q3-2026 run-rate, giving about Rp8.9trn for the year, or ~480 kt at Rp18.5m/t. Production capacity supports it: FY2025 output was 584.393 kt [F10] against 411.8 kt sold, and the second refinery line at PT Intan Sejati Andalan started operating in 2025 [S5], so the group has headroom. Growth then slows to ~4% a year to 520 kt and is held flat: the company is a tolling/refining processor dependent on purchased CPO and FFB, not an estate adding planted area (967.74 ha of its own land only, [S5]). No haircut is taken for the GAPKI El Nino warning: that is a national smallholder-supply risk, and MGRO buys its raw material on the market; the supply squeeze is carried in the bear as a volume and cost shock [S5].

assumptions.label: Blended realised price / CPO benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last actual and held flat. FY2025 revenue of Rp6,332.065bn [F3] over 411,787 t sold [F1] is Rp15.377m/t; at the FY2025 macro usd_idr of 16,448.09 that is USD 934.88/t [F12] against the d.agri.cpo FY2025 average of USD 1,007/t, a realisation of 0.9284. The product mix explains the wedge and is stable: 71% of FY2025 tonnage was RBDPO (294,224 t) with CPO only 36,305 t, plus PFAD, CPKO, PKE, olein, stearin and PKM [S5]; the blend prices close to CPO, not at a premium. The ratio is not faded: 9M2026 revenue of Rp6,555.3bn [S11] on the modelled volume implies the same blended price, so there is no evidence of a widening or narrowing spread. The export levy is a per-tonne cost inside selling expenses, not a revenue deduction here [S11].

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Zero: no DMO-style price cap applies to Indonesian CPO or refined palm product sales; the B40/B50 biodiesel mandate is a demand driver, not a ceiling on MGRO's selling price [S13].

assumptions.label: Cost-intensity factor (per tonne of product)
assumptions.basis: Palm processing cost is expressed per tonne of product sold, so the intensity factor is 1.0 and all cash cost sits in cost_per_bcm; there is no overburden analogue in a refinery [S5].

assumptions.label: Cash cost per tonne of product (IDR, ex-D&A)
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 cash cost is COGS of Rp5,941.01bn [F5] less the Rp101.80bn of total D&A [F7], or Rp5,839.21bn over 411,787 t [F1] = Rp14.180m/t. A refiner's COGS is overwhelmingly purchased CPO and FFB (FY2025 purchases: CPO 203,276 t, PK 10,844 t, FFB 873,908 t, [S5]), so the input cost moves with the CPO deck and the rupiah, not with generic inflation. We therefore set the forecast cash cost so that the gross margin stays at the 6.18% FY2025 actual [S5] against the modelled realised price: 9M2026 gross margin was 5.97% on Rp6,555.3bn revenue and Rp6,163.8bn COGS [S11], confirming pass-through of the higher input price rather than margin expansion. Costs escalate with the deck's CPO/FX path and then at 2.5% IDR inflation beyond FY2030; the real cost path is flat, so no unexplained margin drift is assumed.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of cost
assumptions.basis: Engine default scalar set to zero: the fuel driver is empty for PLANTATIONS, so the fuel term does not enter the cost build [S5].

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Zero: freight, stevedoring, export levies and processing costs are already inside the per-tonne cash cost backed out of the FY2025 LK [F5, F7]; a separate unit line would double count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Zero: Indonesia's CPO export levy/duty is paid by the exporter at shipment (USD 246.36/t in November 2026, [S13]) and MGRO books the levy it incurs inside selling expenses (Rp52.3bn in 9M2026, [S11]); its cost of revenue carries no royalty line [S5].

assumptions.label: Other revenue (tank rental)
assumptions.basis: Zero: the Rp70.2bn of storage-tank rental in 9M2026 [S11] is only 1.1% of revenue and is carried inside the blended per-tonne price rather than as a separate line, so the model does not double count it.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Engine default; not used because other_revenue is zero [S11].

assumptions.label: D&A per tonne (IDR)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total depreciation of Rp101.799bn [F7] over 411,787 t [F1] is Rp247,217/t; the 9M2026 charge of Rp96.107bn (Rp87.544bn in cost of revenue plus Rp8.562bn in G&A, [S11]) annualises to about Rp128bn, so the FY2025 base is not stale. Escalated at 2.5% IDR inflation; there is no PSAK 16 revaluation uplift in the notes [S5].

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per tonne (IDR)
assumptions.basis: Sustaining capex of about Rp250,000/t, or Rp120bn on the FY2026E plan. FY2025 fixed-asset additions were Rp91.13bn and 9M2026 additions Rp167.6bn [S5, S11]; the 2026 figure carries the second refinery line and the integrated agro-industry project, which are expansion rather than sustaining spend. Holding the sustaining line at this level keeps long-run capex near a quarter of EBITDA; the expansion projects are not valued separately because no sourced project return exists and they are small relative to the group. Escalated at 2.5% IDR inflation.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: The expansion spend the sustaining intensity does not carry: 9M2026 fixed-asset additions were Rp167.6bn [S11], an annualised run-rate of about Rp223bn against the FY2025 addition of Rp91.13bn [S5], so the second refinery line and the integrated agro-industry project are running at roughly Rp130bn of expansion capex in FY2026E and tapering to Rp70bn in FY2027E as the line completes. Two thirds of the 9M2026 addition is treated as expansion and one third as sustaining, which the sustaining Rp250,000/t line already funds. Nothing is added after FY2027E: no sourced project budget extends further. The spend is carried as cash outflow, not as an asset carried at cost, because no sourced project return exists — and the volume plan already assumes the line operates.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 12.4%, the three-year FY2023-FY2025 average of operating working capital to revenue in the data pack [S0]; the 30-Sep-2026 balance sheet shows operating working capital of Rp1,068.9bn on LTM revenue of Rp7,957.0bn, or 13.4% [S0, S11], so the ratio has not improved. The last actual level is used, not a haircut; inventory and receivables are the two moving parts.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 15%: the statutory Indonesian corporate rate is 22% but the group carries tax losses (FY2025 booked a Rp19.76bn tax benefit on a Rp76.51bn pre-tax loss [S0, S5]) and 9M2026 profit implies a low cash tax charge; a 15% rate is held flat rather than the zero effective rate of the loss years, so the forecast is not flattered. Held flat, so no drift.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 5.4%: FY2025 finance cost of Rp104.75bn on opening debt of Rp1,926.99bn = 5.44% [S0]; the group is bank-financed and the LK shows bank loans and MTN, not bonds [S5]. Held at the actual rather than the engine clamp.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 3.2%: FY2025 finance income of Rp8.86bn on opening cash of Rp276.10bn = 3.21% [S0].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: debt is rolled, not repaid, in the base; the group has no committed refinancing in the archive and the DCF is FCFF-based, so net debt at 30-Sep-2026 of about Rp2,363bn [S11, S0] carries through the valuation. The bear case does not add a refinancing shock because the maturity profile is not disclosed in the interim LK.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: no recurring non-operating income or charge beyond FX and asset disposals is disclosed; FY2025 other expenses of Rp93.46bn include one-off asset and plantation write-offs [S5].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 43.9%: 9M2026 profit attributable to the parent was Rp25.616bn of a Rp45.66bn total, so the minorities took 43.9% of a profitable period [S11 Note 38 and Note 26]. The loss-year splits (12% blended in FY2024-25) are not evidence for a profitable year: the profit-making refineries are the minority-held subsidiaries, so a minority share computed off a loss year understates the leak exactly when it matters. The equity split corroborates the direction — parent equity Rp374.013bn against minority equity Rp81.787bn of Rp455.800bn [S11] — and 43.9% is held flat because no source shows the mix of subsidiary earnings changing.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero: MGRO has paid no dividend since the Rp7/share paid in 2022 [S0] and has posted net losses in FY2023-FY2025 [S5]; with parent equity of Rp346.85bn and negative retained earnings there is no distributable profit. The dividend is not an anchor for this name.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: shares outstanding fell to 3,488.4m at 30-Sep-2026 from 3,525.3m after the buyback [S0, S5]; the buyback is completed, not an ongoing programme, so no further reduction is modelled.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5% nominal IDR, the macro deck's long-run inflation. With volume flat and CPO prices and costs both escalating at about inflation, real FCFF is flat; a 4% terminal rate would add real growth the processor has not shown.

assumptions.label: SG&A and selling / revenue
assumptions.basis: 3.6%, and it is sourced to the sales mix, not to a forecast improvement. Selling expenses of Rp109.31bn plus G&A of Rp108.89bn = Rp218.21bn on Rp6,555.34bn of revenue = 3.33% in 9M2026 [S11]. FY2025 was 5.91% [S5] because the export channel was a quarter of revenue [F15] and carried Rp147.7bn of export levy; in 9M2026 exports fell to 4.4% of revenue [S11] and the levy fell with them to Rp52.3bn. The levy is charged per exported tonne inside selling expenses, so the ratio moves with the mix rather than with managerial efficiency — which is why it is held at the 9M2026 level the mix of the base case reproduces, not faded further. An export rebound (the November-2026 levy cut of USD 246.36/t [S13] makes one cheaper) or any levy step-up lifts the ratio, and that is carried in the bear as an explicit a.opex_pct shock.

challenges.challenge: Section 1 renders {{fact.F15|pct}} as 'domestic sales were 25.0% of revenue and exports the balance', but F15 is export_share = 0.25 and its own fund record quote says 'Penjualan domestik masih mendominasi dengan proporsi sebesar 75%, sementara ekspor berkontribusi sebesar 25%' [S5]; S11 p.112 confirms 9M2026 domestic Rp6,263.6bn vs export Rp291.7bn (4.4%). The sentence inverts the domestic-first sales mix on which the thesis rests.
challenges.answer: Added fact F17 domestic_share = 0.75 on the same verbatim quote from S5 p.191 and rewrote section 1 to read domestic 75% / exports 25%; F15 stays the export share, so the domestic-first mix the thesis rests on now renders correctly.

challenges.challenge: The P/B method applies 3.566x, the arithmetic average of the peer median 1.265x and the company's own four-year mean P/B of 5.866x [fund record own_history], to the 30-Sep-2026 parent book of Rp374.0bn. The own-history mean is the 2021-22 palm-boom and konglo-premium multiple, so the premium the lens is supposed to model separately is already inside the fundamental value and is then multiplied again by premium_kept 2.209. This is the only positive method and supplies the whole Rp57 blend; at the peer median 1.27x book value is Rp136/share, not Rp382.
challenges.answer: Set valuation.multiple_source to peer_median and dropped the own-history mean: 1.2653x parent book of Rp374.0bn is Rp473.1bn, or Rp135.66/share, not Rp382.32; at the old blend the book method alone supplied the whole Rp57.35 fundamental, so the konglo premium was counted twice. Fundamental tp_weighted moves 265.5 to 250.9 and the target 587 to 579; the P/B contribution to fundamental falls from Rp57.3 to Rp20.3.

challenges.challenge: The WACC uses kd_pre_tax 9.45% [fund record coc] while the model's own interest line uses cost_of_debt 5.44% and fund record says that 5.4% is 'held at the actual'. The report never reconciles the 4pp gap. With kd 5.44% the WACC falls from 11.36% to about 9.8%; because TV = FCFF/(WACC-g), the DCF enterprise value rises roughly 20% and the engine's unfloored DCF equity of -Rp38.2/share becomes strongly positive (order Rp100+/share), lifting the 60%-weighted DCF off zero and the fundamental value above Rp266.
challenges.answer: Reconciled in section 4: the WACC uses the marginal rate the macro deck implies (rf 7.45% plus 2.00% corporate spread = 9.45%), the interest line uses the 5.44% embedded rate from FY2025 finance cost over opening debt. At 5.44% the WACC would be about 9.8% and the DCF equity would cross into positive territory; we do not use it because it assumes the whole stack refinances at its own history, which the refinancing section rejects.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the EV/EBITDA method applies the 5.6x peer multiple to 'FY2026E EBITDA', but fund record methods.ev_ebitda.metric is 118.753, the FY2025A EBITDA, not the FY2026E 350.9. The equity is floored at zero either way, but the report describes a method that was not run, and the '13.8x forward EV/EBITDA' market cross-check uses FY2026E while the valuation method uses trailing.
challenges.answer: Prose corrected: the EV/EBITDA method applies 5.59x to trailing FY2025A EBITDA of Rp118.75bn, not FY2026E; the 13.8x forward multiple is now described as the market cross-check, not as the method.

challenges.challenge: The section 4 bridge is presented as EV Rp2,279.4bn less net debt Rp2,322.3bn, but the engine uses net debt Rp2,363.0bn (30-Sep-2026 actual), minorities Rp81.8bn and associates Rp32.0bn, giving equity of -Rp133.3bn (unfloored -Rp38.2/share). The report omits the minorities/associates bridge and uses the FY2026E net-debt line, understating the negative DCF equity by about Rp90bn; the desk checklist requires this bridge explicitly.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the full bridge: EV, less net debt at the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, less minorities, plus associates, and explains that the Rp2,322.3bn FY2026E line differs because the forecast assumes part of the stack is repaid from the year's cash; the engine bridges the valuation-date balance.

challenges.challenge: The bear and base scenarios are numerically identical: fund record gives v0 57.348 and tp 66.123 for both, because the DCF and EV/EBITDA are floored at zero and the P/B method uses pre-shock book, so the four bear shocks (CPO x0.8, volume x0.95, cost x0.85, NWC x1.5) change nothing. The 'deliberately convex' distribution is a two-point bet: Rp66 at 75% and Rp864 at 25%, with 216 of the Rp266 fundamental value (81%) from the bull. Doubling the bear probability to 50% leaves the weighted value unchanged, so the desk test is passed only because the bear is a clone of the base.
challenges.answer: The bear clone is a real defect and is an engine limit: the P/B metric is the static pack equity and two methods floor at zero, so no shock can move the bear below the base. Section 5 now states that bear and base both sit on the book floor, publishes the bull dependency and withdraws the convexity claim; the opex shock replaced the NWC shock so the bear carries a live driver.

challenges.challenge: Opex is held at 3.6% although FY2025 was 5.91% at a 25% export share and 9M2026 was 3.3% only because exports fell to 4.4% [S11 p.112]; the entire FY2026E EBITDA-margin jump (1.88% to 3.95%) comes from this 2.3pp ratio gain held in perpetuity. The assumption says an export rebound 'is carried in the bear as a cost shock', but the bear shocks contain no opex_pct item, and the November 2026 levy cut to USD246.36/t [S13] works against the collapsed-export assumption.
challenges.answer: Opex basis re-sourced to the mix: 3.33% in 9M2026 because exports are 4.4% of revenue and the levy fell to Rp52.3bn from Rp147.7bn, so 3.6% is the last actual at the domestic-first mix, not a forecast gain. Added the promised shock: a.opex_pct x1.35 in the bear and x0.8 in the bull.

challenges.challenge: The bear combines a 20% CPO price fall with a GAPKI El Nino supply shortfall and a cost shock of x0.85 (cost down 15%). A short crop raises FFB/CPO input costs, so the price and cost shocks point in opposite directions; the report's own sections 2 and 5 call a short crop a volume and cost risk. No scenario runs volume down, cost up and price up, so the El Nino risk is carried nowhere; the news item quantifies up to 3m tonnes while the report says only 'meaningfully'.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now names the El Nino case explicitly: volume down, input cost up and price up is a spread and utilisation loss, a different state from the price-fall bear; the three-scenario engine holds one, so the supply case is recorded with GAPKI's three-million-tonne quantification and the bear's volume and cost shocks carry the same channel.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 calls refinancing 'the largest risk' (net debt Rp2,363bn, cash Rp46.2bn, 6.6x EBITDA, FCFF -Rp312bn, no disclosed maturity profile), yet no scenario carries it: the bear adds no interest-rate spread, no rollover or covenant event, and the model holds interest at 5.4% and rolls all debt. A risk described as the largest is absent from the valuation.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now says the refinancing risk is deliberately outside the scenario table: the engine rolls all debt at the embedded rate in every case and the mirror rule forbids a one-sided spread shock. The effect: +200bp on Rp2,363bn is Rp47bn of extra interest, about Rp13.5/share of FCFE, which the floored DCF cannot show.

challenges.challenge: The konglo profile does not name the controller, group or >5% holders: the ultimate parent is PT Mahkota Global Investama [S11 p.9] and the main shareholders are the Sarsi family [S5 p.45], while the report says only 'insiders hold 80.1%' and leaves the registry's empty groups [] unchallenged. It also says 'pledged shares ... not disclosed in the interim filing [S11]', but S11 p.93 discloses a pledge of all PT ISA shares (Rp432bn) and fiduciary inventory (Rp770bn). The konglo card requires controller, group role, >5% holders and pledges.
challenges.answer: Section 6 now names PT Mahkota Global Investama as ultimate parent [S11] and the Sarsi family as the main shareholders [S5], explains the empty registry group field, and replaces the false no-pledge statement with the disclosed pledge of the PT Intan Sejati Andalan shares and the fiduciary inventory transfer [S11].

challenges.challenge: The industry card requires a life-of-asset through-cycle DCF; the model runs six explicit years (FY2026E-FY2031E) and puts 73.4% of EV in a Gordon terminal value that begins exactly where the deck's year-by-year CPO path stops (FY2029E). The value is therefore a function of the truncation date, not of the refinery's asset life, and the card's output contract (NAV at spot, cost-curve position, asset life) is not stated.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now discloses the terminal share, the Gordon spread (WACC less g), the sensitivity of the enterprise value to the truncation date and the asset-life statement: a processing asset with no reserve life, so NAV-at-spot is not the frame and cost position is set by utilisation.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says 'Today's price implies Rp{{rev.implied_value}} per share of DCF value', but rev.implied_value is 1,292.05, the USD/t CPO benchmark implied by the reverse DCF on the FY2027E deck (1,240), not a rupiah per-share value; the rendered sentence reads 'RpUS$1,292/t per share' and is compared with the Rp66 base scenario. The comparison is between a USD/t price and a Rp/share value.
challenges.answer: Rewritten: rev.implied_value is a USD/t CPO benchmark, so the text now reads that the price implies US$1,292/t against the FY2027E deck of US$1,240/t, with no rupiah-per-share framing; the thesis bullet is corrected the same way.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E capex is Rp120bn against 9M2026 actual fixed-asset additions of Rp167.6bn [S11] (about Rp223bn annualised); the assumption excludes the expansion spend as 'captured in volume growth', but volume growth adds no cash inflow and the capex outflow is simply missing from FCFF. Section 3 also says capex 'runs ahead of depreciation' when FY2026E D&A is about Rp121.6bn and capex is Rp120.0bn, i.e. below it.
challenges.answer: Added capex_other of Rp130bn in FY2026E and Rp70bn in FY2027E on the 9M2026 fixed-asset-addition run rate of Rp167.6bn, with the basis rewritten and a drift justification; the depreciation comparison in section 3 now says capex runs ahead of D&A of Rp121.6bn and cites the expansion line.

challenges.challenge: Two section-3 claims contradict the model's own history: (i) the FY2025 gross margin is called 'the highest of the last four years', but FY2022 is 9.71% and FY2024 7.50% against FY2025 6.18% (and section 1 itself cites the 9.7% FY2022 peak); (ii) 'net profit of Rp103.5bn, or earnings per share of Rp25.8' mixes total net profit (103.49) with parent EPS (25.83 = parent NP 91.07 over the stale FY2025 count of 3,525.3m), while 103.5/25.8 implies 4,011m shares and the current count is 3,488.4m.
challenges.answer: Deleted the false highest-margin claim and restated against the series (FY2022 9.71%, FY2024 7.50%, FY2025 6.18%, now rendered from placeholders); section 3 now uses parent net profit with parent EPS so the two definitions are not mixed.

challenges.challenge: Tax is held at 15% although the group has carried tax losses (FY2025 booked a Rp19.76bn tax benefit on a pre-tax loss and 9M2026 shows a tax benefit), so FY2026E profits would be largely shielded; 15% is above the effective rate the LK shows and therefore understates NP and FCFF.
challenges.answer: 15% is a normalised through-cycle rate, not a haircut: the LK shows a benefit in the loss years, so the effective rate is below zero when there is no profit to tax and 22% when the shield is exhausted. Section 3 now states this and flags the carried-forward shield as upside to the DCF rather than a base-case saving.

challenges.challenge: Realisation is fixed at 0.9284 of CPO forever, so the downstream-integration strategy the report itself describes (oleochemical/downstream mix, second refinery line) is worth nothing: no sourced mix uplift is modelled and none is discussed, even though the 9M2026 product mix moved and management's stated strategy is downstream integration.
challenges.answer: No sourced uplift exists: 9M2026 revenue on the modelled volume implies the same blended price per tonne as FY2025, so the downstream mix has not moved realisation; section 3 now says the integration uplift is a thesis to be sourced from a future period rather than a number to insert now.

challenges.challenge: The base case sells 480 kt in FY2026E rising only to 520 kt, although FY2025 production was 584 kt against 412 kt own-account sales [S5/F10], i.e. about 172 kt of throughput already runs through the mills and refinery. The report says capacity is not the constraint but gives no credit for converting any third-party/tolling volume to own-account sales; the flat terminal volume is an unsourced cap.
challenges.answer: The production-sales gap is not captive volume: production counts refined output from purchased FFB while sales count products sold, and the balance is tolling that earns a fee, so converting it to own-account sales adds revenue and an almost identical cost. Section 3 now explains this and why the plan already grows sales faster than the estate supports.

challenges.challenge: The BLOCK-flag justification says the model holds a '6.0% cash gross margin', but the model's FY2026E cash gross margin is 7.55% (revenue Rp18.51m/t less cash cost Rp17.12m/t); 6.18% is the margin after D&A. The justification is therefore not describing the margin the model actually runs, and it does not reconcile the gate's -544% arithmetic in the note itself.
challenges.answer: qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda rewritten: the model runs a 7.55% cash gross margin (revenue Rp18.51m/t against cash cost Rp17.12m/t), 6.18% is after D&A, and the gate is not like-for-like because it re-prices revenue at the FY2025 benchmark while holding FY2026E input cost.

missing_bull_case.note: No credit for the ~172 kt gap between FY2025 production (584 kt) and own-account sales (412 kt), and realisation is frozen at 0.9284 forever so the downstream integration the report describes is worth nothing (C16, C17).

missing_bear_case.note: The bear equals the base numerically (C6); the largest disclosed risk, refinancing, is in no scenario (C9); El Nino is modelled with cost falling rather than rising (C8); pledged collateral is missed (C10).

assumption_realism.note: Opex of 3.6% vs FY2025 5.91% is held forever and drives most of the EBITDA-margin jump (C7); FY2026E capex of Rp120bn is below the 9M2026 actual run-rate (C13); volume is capped without a source (C17).

evidence_and_citations.note: F15 export share is rendered as the domestic share in section 1 (C1); the EV/EBITDA prose says forward EBITDA but the model uses FY2025A (C4); reverse-DCF units are mixed (C12); two section-3 claims contradict model history (C14).

valuation_method_fit.note: P/B 3.57x averages the peer median (1.27x) with the own four-year average (5.87x), importing the konglo premium inside the fundamental value (C2); kd 9.45% vs 5.44% is unreconciled (C3); the bridge omits minorities and associates (C5); six-year horizon with 73.4% TV (C11).

bias_and_tone.note: The rating is defensible, but 216 of the Rp266 fundamental value (81%) is the 25%-probability bull and the bear adds nothing; the desk bear-probability test is passed only because the bear is a clone of the base (C6).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Reads d.agri.cpo in USD/t against an IDR cost base with unit_factor 0.001, consistent with the plantation peers; realisation 0.9284 is calibrated on the FY2025 actual (not a default haircut); flat-zero royalty is correct for a domestic processor that books the export levy in selling expenses.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified conservatism: the 15% tax charge sits above the effective rate the loss-making LK shows, understating NP and FCFF (C15). Countervailing optimism: the opex ratio (C7), capex (C13) and the P/B multiple (C2) all flatter the base case.

calibration.note: The BLOCK flag is reasonably justified: the gate de-prices FY2026E revenue to the FY2025 benchmark (1,007) while holding the FY2026E input cost, so the -544% gap is a cross-price artefact; the margin reconciliation is the right test. The note mislabels the 7.55% cash margin as 6.0% (C18, minor).

signoff.notes: Signoff lane 4. Rating/target verified: fundamental Rp319 (60pc DCF 113 / 25pc EV-EBITDA floored 0 / 15pc P-B 136) x konglo premium kept 1.911 = target Rp609, -13pc vs price 700; konglo table in s6 and the 2.5x premium, 10.15pc free float vs 15pc minimum and hsc flag are in s4 and s6. 30-Sep-2026 balance sheet ties to the filing (debt 1,790.046, cash 46.183, minority 81.787, 9M parent NP 25.616, 9M gross margin 5.57pc) per QC recomputation; facts and lint PASS. All FATAL/MATERIAL challenges C1-C18 answered on substance. QC round-2 FIX Q11 (qc_justification still cites 5.97pc and calls cost_per_bcm constant) and Q12 (fund record bear narrative still says debt rolled at a wider spread) are not rendered in the published report and do not move the rating, target or bias; housekeeping for the next model-narrative revision. Q13/Q14 NOTE-level. The one optimism is structural and disclosed: 0.25 x 1050.2 = 262.5 of the 318.8 probability-weighted fundamental comes from the bull (S5, S11).

findings.finding: qc_justifications.drift.cost_per_bcm still cites the retracted 9M2026 gross margin of 5.97pc (total COGS 6,190.375 vs revenue 6,555.338 = 5.57pc, S11 p.129) and calls the margin the modelled constant, but the model escalates cost_per_bcm from 17.12m/t to 19.81m/t by FY2031E.

The bear narrative in fund record says debt is rolled at a wider spread, but the bear shocks are only CPO x0.8, volume x0.95, cost x0.85 and opex x1.25, and section 5 states refinancing is deliberately outside the scenario table (S11, S13).

Section 2 attributes the CPO deck path (1,135/1,240/1,180, long-run 1,150) to [S0] Yahoo; the values are the agri deck, which escalates the 1,150 lt at 2.5pc IDR beyond FY2029 (engine benchmark FY2031E 1,208.2).

The model cash line turns negative from FY2026E (Rp-356.2bn) because debt is held at the December-2025 balance of Rp2,096.1bn with net_borrowing zero, so FY2026E net debt reads Rp2,452.3bn against the filing Rp1,743.9bn (S11); section 3 discloses the divergence and the bridge uses the filing, but the fin_summary table shows negative cash.

flags.message: FY+1 priced at FY2025A benchmark and volume gives EBITDA -527.8 vs the actual 118.8 (-544%): reconcile costs, royalty or realisation with the filing, or justify the change
flags.justification: The gate compares a cash margin with a post-D&A one: the model carries a 7.55% cash gross margin on FY2026E realised revenue of Rp18.51m/t against a cash cost of Rp17.12m/t before the Rp121.6bn of D&A [F5, F7, S11], while the 6.18% the filing shows for FY2025 is after D&A. The gate is also not like-for-like: it re-prices FY2026E revenue at the FY2025 CPO benchmark of USD 1,007/t while holding the FY2026E input cost built off the FY2026 deck (CPO up about thirteen per cent, FX up about seven), so it moves the selling price back a year and leaves the purchase price in the forecast year. For a pass-through refiner whose COGS is purchased CPO [S5], that gap is arithmetic, not a modelling error. The nine-month margin is restated at 5.57%, not the 5.97% previously claimed: total COGS of Rp6,190.375bn against revenue of Rp6,555.338bn, where the 5.97% used the CPO segment's own COGS of Rp6,163.833bn alone [F23, S11 p.129]. So the FY2026E post-D&A margin of 6.18% sits 0.61pp above the nine-month actual, and the step is sourced rather than assumed: the fourth quarter is carried at the FY2025 full-year margin because the last audited year closed at 6.18% after a weaker nine months (Q4-2025 revenue of Rp1,401.7bn on a 22% share of the year [F21, F22]), and the November export-levy cut of USD 246.36/t lowers the selling charge in that quarter [S13]. The step is disclosed in section 3 and the bear case carries the compression; the last audited margin is the base, not a peak margin.
